The Nobel Foundation has allowed selection committees to deviate from Nobel’s stipulation that the achievement for which the prize is awarded be in the preceding year. The committees have given prizes for discoveries made decades before the year of the award. Penicillin, for example, was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 and developed into a drug by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in the early 1940s, and the award was given to the three in 1945. Peyton Rous, the oldest awardee, received the prize in 1966 at age 87 for work reported in 1910, 56 years earlier, on a transmissible (viral-induced) sarcoma in fowl. The Nobel Prize, especially in Physiology or Medicine, has in recent decades more often been given as an award shared by two or three scientists. The Nobel Foundation has agreed that no more than three awardees can share a single prize. Each awardee receives his or her medal and diploma; however, the monetary award is divided equally among them.

## THE NOBEL PRIZE IN PHYSIOLOGY OR MEDICINE

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, because of its relationship to human health and well-being, is the one that can be identified most readily by the public as meeting Nobel’s intent to recognize the accomplishment that is a benefit to mankind. The prize in physiology or medicine has not been awarded every year. For example, no prizes were offered for several years during the First and Second World War and in several years in which an appropriate candidate was not identified. From 1901 to 2016, 107 awards have been made to 210 laureates, of whom 12 were women.20,21 Approximately one-third of the prizes were given to one laureate, one-third was shared by two awardees, and one-third was shared by three awardees. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded without interruption from 1943 to 2016.

Prior to World War II, Europe was the center of scientific research, and European scientists received most of the prizes for physiology or medicine. From 1901 to 1939, only three prizes for physiology or medicine were won or shared by North Americans: the first to Canadians, Frederick Banting and John James Rickard Macleod, for the isolation and clinical use of insulin in 1923; the second to Thomas Hunt Morgan for his early studies of genetics and inheritance, pioneering the use of _Drosophila melanogaster_ (the fruit fly) for genetic research; and the third in 1934, for the cure of pernicious anemia, was shared by George Richards Minot, William Parry Murphy, and George Hoyt Whipple, to be discussed subsequently in this paper.

Following the Second World War, with the massive disruption and destruction in Europe and the establishment of the National Science Foundation and the expansion of the National Institutes of Health, the United States became the home of the most generously supported and largest biomedical research establishment in the world. From 1943 until the current time, over 70% of the laureates in physiology or medicine have been either native or naturalized US citizens.

In the pre-World War II period, 42 of the 45 laureates in physiology or medicine held a medical degree, and many practiced medicine. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine reflected successes in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century in conquering diseases caused by microbes and elucidating major physiologic functions of the body. Robert Koch, Paul Ehrlich, Élie Metchnikoff (one of only two Russian, more specifically Ukrainian, laureates in physiology or medicine), Jules Bordet, Ivan Pavlov (the other Russian), and Karl Landsteiner are only a few of the laureates on the list, which is a treasure trove of great European physicians of the late nineteenth and early twentieth century.

Following the Second World War, the awards began to focus on fundamental biochemical or molecular discoveries—including such areas as the physical and chemical basis of nerve conduction, the chemical basis of vision, investigations of tumor viruses, the genetic basis of atherosclerosis, the action of cell growth factors, the cellular origin of cancer genes, the fundamentals of bacterial or viral genetics, DNA replication in bacteria, the structure of DNA, the biosynthesis of DNA and RNA, pluripotential stem cell biology, basic elements of the immune system, and so on—making the direct benefit to mankind demanded by Nobel’s will less apparent to the lay observer and certainly less immediate.

Despite the focus on basic discoveries, at least two awards in the modern era were made to practicing physicians: the 1990 prize shared by Edward Donnall Thomas, an oncologist, and Joseph Edward Murray, a transplant surgeon, for the development of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and renal transplantation, paving the way for liver, heart, lung, and other solid organ transplantation. The 2005 award was shared by a clinical pathologist, John Robin Warren, and an internist-gastroenterologist, Barry James Marshall, for the discovery of _Helicobacter pylori_ and its role in gastric inflammation and peptic ulcer development. Later the organism was shown to cause gastric carcinoma and gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma.

One Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded for what proved to be erroneous research, the award in 1926 to Johannes Andreas Grib Fibiger, a Danish professor of pathological anatomy, who reported the discovery of a worm that caused cancer of the rat stomach, which he designated _Spiroptera carcinoma_. The lesions were later shown to be hyperplastic, not neoplastic.18 Remarkably, three reports that were contemporaneous with Fibiger’s showing that coal tar produced cancer of the skin of animals; that a putative cancer virus could transmit fowl tumors; and that _Schistosoma haematobium_ infection can result in bladder cancer were overlooked.22 The discovery of a transmissible agent that caused fowl sarcoma by Peyton Rous was recognized by the Nobel Foundation approximately a half century later. Each of these three mechanisms of cancer initiation has stood the test of time.

A second prize may have been premature, and certainly controversial, namely the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to António Egas Moniz, a Portuguese neurologist, for the treatment of severe psychiatric disorders, especially schizophrenia, by prefrontal lobotomy.23 The prize was shared with Walter Rudolf Hess for his neurophysiological studies of the diencephalon. A notable victim of the lobotomy procedure was Rosemary Kennedy, sister of US President John Fitzgerald Kennedy, an attractive, interactive woman, whose functional state was converted to a vegetative state by the procedure inflicted on her at the insistence of her father in 1941.

Today, with a research establishment that spans the world and with several hundred accomplished nominees each year, it is very difficult to award the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine to the most deserving scientist or physician. Indeed, laureates recognize that their work would not have been possible without the discoveries of other scientists whose work had not been recognized by the Foundation.24 A former chairman of the Nobel Foundation, Arne Tiselius, himself a laureate, in response to a query about how laureates are selected, indicated that one cannot in practice apply the principle that the Nobel Prize should be given to the person who is best; it is impossible to define who is best. Hence, there is only one alternative: to try to find a particularly worthy candidate.

The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded in 1934 for the treatment of pernicious anemia holds special significance for the University of Rochester School of Medicine and Dentistry, which was nine years old in 1934, the first post-Flexnerian medical school established in the United States, when its founding Dean, George Whipple, shared the prize for his work on the repair of anemia in chronically bled dogs and the importance of liver in the diet to repair the anemia most efficiently.25

In the late nineteenth and early twentieth century, patients in North America and Europe with an eventually fatal type of severe anemia were being described. The affected patients also had severe neurologic damage, and the outcome of the disease, although more protracted, was similar to adults with acute leukemia, invariably resulting in death. The patients often had pancytopenia, profoundly proliferative and dysplastic marrow cells, and neurological impairment. In 1908, Richard Cabot of Boston provided a comprehensive clinical description of the disease and an analysis of 1,200 patients. He found that survival after onset was 1 to 3 years.26 The anemia was referred to as “pernicious.”

In 1918, Whipple began his experiments on dogs bled to half normal hemoglobin levels. A basal diet of canned salmon and bread allowed periodic withdrawal of blood to maintain the low blood hemoglobin. If a diet was introduced that contained beef liver or muscle, hemoglobin production increased. Whipple and his co-worker, Frieda Robscheit-Robbins, published a paper in the _American Journal of Physiology_ on blood regeneration and severe anemia in the 1920s that highlighted the favorable influence of liver in the diet on the regeneration of red blood cells in their dog model of anemia. They stated: “Liver feeding in these severe anemias remains the most potent factor for the sustained production of hemoglobin and red cells.”25 In publications in 1922 and 1925, Whipple encouraged physicians to consider dietary factors in the management of anemic patients based on his studies in dogs.25

In 1925, William Murphy had one year earlier gone into medical practice and was on the staff of the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital in Boston. He agreed to work with George Minot, who was a physician-investigator on the faculty of the Harvard Medical School and the Huntington Memorial Hospital, on a project to determine if a form of diet therapy could help patients with pernicious anemia, a disease in which Minot had a special interest. Minot’s view that a dietary factor may play a role in the development of pernicious anemia grew out of the notion that “good food makes good blood,” which was a general theme during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In 1926, Minot and Murphy astounded the world of medicine with the announcement at the meeting of the Association of American Physicians at its annual gathering in Atlantic City that they had cured the anemia in a series of 45 patients. These patients had been fed a special diet that contained up to one-half pound of lightly cooked beef liver, daily, for several months. This was an unappetizing diet, especially in patients seriously ill with loss of appetite and other gastrointestinal disturbances. Nevertheless, the effect of this discovery was not only to reverse the death sentence for these patients but to encourage and stimulate research concerning diseases of the blood.

Minot credited Whipple for highlighting the importance of nutrition as a potential factor in anemic patients and for focusing on liver. In their paper in the _Journal of the American Medical Association_ in 1926, Minot and Murphy reported the salutary effects of liver feeding in pernicious anemia patients. Minot’s and Murphy’s paper had several references to Whipple’s and Robscheit-Robbin’s work and one reference to their own prior work, although none of these prior reports had anything to do with dietary treatment of pernicious anemia.27

Some observers felt that Whipple’s role was not consequential enough to merit his sharing the prize. In a monograph entitled _Anemia in practice: Pernicious anemia_, written by Murphy and published in 1939, he wrote in his chapter entitled “The Introduction of Liver Therapy” that,

> It became our task then to prove the practicability of an idea which had up to this time received no intensive study or definite confirmation. Some years previously Whipple and his co-workers had demonstrated that liver had a rather unusual value for the production of hemoglobin in dogs made anemic by bleeding. Because this worked entirely with the production of hemoglobin as opposed to the maturation of erythrocytes, the latter being the problem chiefly concerned in recovery in pernicious anemia, because it was carried out entirely on animals, rather than human beings, and because the results of the study had no bearing upon or reference to pernicious anemia as observed in mankind, the study which we were to undertake was of a pioneering nature. No background evidence proved that it would be beneficial, except that a few patients who had been advised by Dr. Minot to ingest some liver together with red muscle meat, as part of their diets, had apparently remained in better health during short periods of time, than those who had not used liver.28

Whipple was studying the response of iron deficiency anemia produced by chronic bleeding of his dogs, whereas Minot and Murphy were later shown to be studying vitamin B12 deficiency. Liver was a rich source of iron and vitamin B12 and, thus, reversed the iron deficiency anemia in Whipple’s dogs and the anemia in humans with pernicious anemia by happenstance and for quite different reasons. Minot and Murphy did not know the pathogenesis of pernicious anemia, only that something in liver could reverse its expression. In the context of the late 1920s and early 1930s, this finding justified their selection. They cured a fatal disease. The reason liver feedings worked was that the daily requirement for vitamin B12 is minuscule, approximately one millionth of a gram per day. The vitamin B12 contained in liver is very large in comparison, and sufficient liver was eaten by patients to provide this minuscule amount of vitamin B12 across the intestinal wall by mass action in the absence of intrinsic factor in gastric juice, normally required for vitamin B12’s absorption.

In 1927 and 1928, a Harvard physician-scientist, William Castle, published a series of ingenious experiments in humans showing that a missing factor, secreted by the stomach, which he referred to as an intrinsic factor, was necessary for the absorption of something from food sources to maintain blood production and nervous tissue integrity, including the brain and spinal cord. The factor in food was referred to as the extrinsic factor, later found to be vitamin B12. It was much later determined that pernicious anemia was an autoimmune disease in which an autoimmunological attack was directed at the stomach lining cells leading to gastric atrophy and the inability to secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, normal constituents of the gastric juice. Intrinsic factor is required to complex with vitamin B12 from food sources to permit that vitamin’s absorption in a specific area of the terminal small intestines. Some thought Castle should have shared the Nobel Prize with Minot and Murphy, not Whipple. Vitamin B12 was characterized in 1948 and intrinsic factor in 1961.

Minot had become a severe diabetic as a young adult. He was cared for in Boston by Elliot Joslin with a severely restricted sugar diet. Joslin later founded the Joslin Clinic, a pioneering institution for diabetic care. Minot was alive to make this contribution because of the discovery of insulin in 1922, for which the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded in 1923 to Frederick Banting and John Macleod. The omission of Charles Best, Banting’s colleague in the laboratory, who was integral to the research as one of the awardees in 1923, angered Banting. This dispute was yet another controversy over a Nobel selection decision. Banting shared his monetary award with Best. Because of the long and arduous sea voyage to Stockholm, and an unfamiliar medical environment, a physician accompanied Minot to administer insulin, assist in his rigid low-sugar diet, and to attend to his diabetes, should it go out of control. This medical support allowed him to accept the prize in person, generally a requirement of the Nobel Foundation for receipt of the prize.

Many deserving scientists have been overlooked, too numerous to cite. The so-called forty-first chair is so designated because of the 40 places available in the French Academy; it represents the deserving scientists who just missed selection. For a short period after the establishment of the prizes, the Nobel Foundation published the names of runners-up or honorable mentions, but they stopped doing so. These holders of the forty-first chair include among them people who should have won the prize, but did not, in some cases because they died before their work was recognized as ground-breaking. Since 1974, a Nobel Prize may not be awarded posthumously. Only two prizes were awarded posthumously prior to 1974: one for peace and one for literature. One prize in physiology or medicine was made posthumously because the recipient, Ralph Steinman, working at the Rockefeller University, who discovered the dendritic cell and its function in the immune system, died a few days before the announcement of his selection in October 2011, unbeknownst to the Nobel Foundation. Having made the announcement not knowing he had died, the Foundation proceeded to make the award, posthumously, in that December.

One of the most notable omissions in the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine was Jonas Salk.29 In 1955 the announcement was made that polio was conquered as a result of the singular efforts of Salk to develop, manufacture, and field test the first vaccine. Polio was a scourge in most industrialized countries. In the United States, summers were periods of terror for parents who often kept children from contact with playmates in camps, swimming pools, or sharing a water fountain, and applied other restrictions in the hopes of minimizing viral transmission. The vaccine made unnecessary the need to warehouse the numerous “iron lungs,” respirators used to ventilate children and young adults with “bulbar” polio, previously stored at the ready in most major hospitals for the summer polio season. In July 1960 one iron lung remained at the Strong Memorial Hospital, the University of Rochester Medical Center; it was used it to manage a young man with Guillain–Barré syndrome with respiratory muscle paralysis.

Salk’s work was viewed as applied and only a technical achievement (low-brow) by some of his influential peers. Perhaps, it was not “high science,” but who better would have fit Nobel’s desire to give the prize to someone who benefited mankind in the previous year? This achievement was among the most impactful on human health in the last 70 years. Salk was neither elected to the National Academy of Sciences nor to the American Philosophical Society, although the membership of both organizations included the country’s leading medical investigators.

Some Nobel Prizes in Physics or in Chemistry honored discoveries that later were seen to be important basic contributions to medicine. One of the most important was the initial Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 given to Wilhelm Roentgen for his discovery of a new form of ray, which he called X-rays, using the mathematician’s symbol “X” for its then unknown properties. Few discoveries have had such a profound and lasting impact on medical diagnosis and therapy.

In 1962, Francis Harry Compton Crick, James Dewey Watson, and Maurice Hugh Frederick Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the elucidation of the structure of DNA. Another controversy in the selection of awardees surrounded the omission of Rosalind Franklin whose crystallographic images of DNA were instrumental in deducing its structure. Her X-ray diffraction pictures of DNA taken in a different physical state, not strictly crystalline, established the helical structure of the molecule and that its diameter indicated that it must be made of two intertwined chains. No scientist had imagined DNA had a multi-chained structure. She also corrected the erroneous belief that the phosphate-sugar backbone was in the interior of the molecule with the bases pointing outward. This information was essential for Watson and Crick to build their 3-dimensional model that met the most satisfactory configuration. Their landmark paper was published in the journal _Nature_ in April, 1953, immediately followed in that issue by a paper by Wilkins and another by Franklin. They summed to confirm the double helical structure of DNA, each strand bound together by specific base pairing of nucleotides: adenine and thymine or cytosine and guanine. The paper by Watson and Crick was one page long, a model of brevity in scientific exposition. In retrospect, their paper may have been the most important contribution to the life sciences since Darwin’s book _On the origin of species_ in 1859, 94 years earlier. Yet, it took the Nobel Foundation nearly a decade to honor its significance, by which time Franklin had died of ovarian cancer. She had not been nominated during her lifetime.

In 2013, 51 years after the award, the family of Crick, by then deceased, sold his Nobel Prize medal at auction to the CEO of a Chinese biomedical firm for over two million dollars.30 A seven-page letter by Crick to his 12-year-old son, explaining his discovery, which pre-dated the publication of the seminal paper in _Nature_, was sold to an anonymous buyer for over six million dollars, exceeding by two-fold the previous highest price paid for a letter of historical importance, one written by Abraham Lincoln opposing slavery.31 A year and a half later, James Watson sold his Nobel Prize medal for over four million dollars.32 The proceeds of both sales were intended to be shared with academic institutions important to the careers of both scientists.30,32

## END NOTE

The remarkable persistence of the Nobel Prize as a revered indicator of achievement is a testament to Alfred Nobel’s stipulations and fortune and the Nobel Foundation’s adherence to the highest standards of selection. The prizes remain a measure not only of outstanding individual achievement, but, secondarily, of the ability of a country to provide the environment that permits the free and unencumbered pursuit of truth. The United States has benefited by (1) immigration to this country of outstanding scientists seeking such an environment in which there is scant religious or political pressure on research directions and outcome, (2) the wholesome and fulsome support of research with federal dollars through the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health, and (3) the competitive national process that objectively determines which proposed research has the most sophisticated, insightful, and farsighted scientific ideas for grant awards. Large countries like the former Soviet Union, the current Russian Federation, the People’s Republic of China, other Asian and African countries (e.g. Iran, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Egypt) with people of genius have been underrepresented in awards. It may be that societal and cultural circumstances unfavorable to the support of strong scientific centers, unfettered scientific discovery, and space for unpopular or paradigm-breaking ideas are at play. An analysis has indicated that cultural and familial factors, such as the Judaic tradition of scholarship, may play a role in the development of scientists and writers capable of achievements that benefit mankind, Nobel’s quest.33 Over one-fifth of all Nobel laureates and one-third of all US laureates have been Jewish. Jews represent 0.2% of the world’s population.33 One can ponder and lament how many laureates were lost in Nazi concentration (death) camps among the six million murdered Jews and their descendants.

No sociologist has ever been awarded a Nobel Prize in the strict sense, because there is no Nobel Prize designated for sociology. However, several scholars with strong sociological training or whose work is central to sociology have received Nobel Prizes in other categories (primarily the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences and, more rarely, the Peace Prize). Relevant examples and context:

Why no “Nobel Prize in Sociology”

*   Alfred Nobel’s will established prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Medicine (Physiology), Literature, and Peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel (commonly called the Nobel Prize in Economics) was created in 1968 and is administered like the others, but sociology was never created as a separate category.

Notable sociologists or sociologically influential scholars who won Nobel-type prizes

*   Gunnar Myrdal (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1974): Trained as an economist, Myrdal’s work bridged social policy, institutions, and race—widely cited in social science and sociology.
*   Friedrich Hayek (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1974): Economist by training but engaged with social theory; influential in sociology of knowledge and institutional analysis debates.
*   Amartya Sen (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1998): Economist whose capability approach and work on welfare, development, and social choice have been extensively adopted by sociologists.
*   Douglass North (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1993): Economic historian; his institutional analysis influenced sociological studies of institutions and organizations.
*   Elinor Ostrom (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 2009): Political economist whose work on common-pool resources intersects with sociology, political sociology, and collective action theory.
*   John Hume (Nobel Peace Prize, 1998): Political leader whose work in peace-building has overlap with sociological studies of conflict and social movements.
*   Pope John Paul II (Nobel Peace Prize nominations/discussions, not a laureate): included here as clarification—several prominent sociological figures were influential in peace-related activities though not laureates.

Other relevant laureates with sociological impact

*   Herbert A. Simon (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1978): Work on decision-making, organizations, and bounded rationality is foundational for organizational sociology.
*   Robert Fogel and Douglass North (both economics laureates): Their cliometric and institutional approaches have been used by sociologists studying historical sociology and institutions.

How sociologists are recognized instead

*   Prestigious sociology awards: American Sociological Association (ASA) awards, the Erasmus Prize, Holberg Prize, and various discipline-specific honors are primary recognition venues for sociologists.
*   Interdisciplinary prizes: Many sociologists receive major prizes in economics, political science, or peace-related awards when their work crosses disciplinary boundaries.

Takeaway

*   No Nobel Prize specifically for sociology exists, so no laureate is formally a “Nobel Prize in Sociology” winner. Several Nobel laureates come from neighboring disciplines or produced work that substantially influenced sociology; when sociology crosses into economics, peace studies, or literature, those contributions sometimes earn Nobel recognition.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

Jindal Institute of Behavioural Sciences offers students internship opportunities that often lead to employment, especially for those interested in Child Psychology.

The institute mainly focuses on field learning programmes, and hence the students get to work within organisations right from the first semester, where they can directly engage with children, understand their developmental concerns, and help with mental health and wellbeing.

A number of students from the Applied Psychology programme at JIBS have completed their internships with NGOs and social impact organisations such as Child Rights and You (CRY), Bal Raksha Bharat, Pehchan, and India Vision Foundation.

Students inclined towards clinical or therapeutic work also intern at healthcare and rehabilitation centres, including the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Hopes Autism Centre, and Hope Trust Psychiatric Clinic.

Through these placements, they gain practical experience in psychological assessment, behaviour management, and working closely with children and their families.

In addition, there are opportunities in corporate and organisational sectors where students apply psychological skills such as behavioural analysis, basic counselling, and communication within HR, learning and development, or CSR teams. These types of roles are valuable for those interested in child-focused programmes within larger institutional systems.

Some students also join short-term global programmes offered by JIBS. This could involve visits to schools, community-based institutions, or research facilities.

JIBS offers a range of internship programmes that help Child Psychology students develop effective skill sets in clinical and community settings.

No sociologist has ever been awarded a Nobel Prize in the strict sense, because there is no Nobel Prize designated for sociology. However, several scholars with strong sociological training or whose work is central to sociology have received Nobel Prizes in other categories (primarily the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences and, more rarely, the Peace Prize). Relevant examples and context:

Why no “Nobel Prize in Sociology”

*   Alfred Nobel’s will established prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Medicine (Physiology), Literature, and Peace. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel (commonly called the Nobel Prize in Economics) was created in 1968 and is administered like the others, but sociology was never created as a separate category.

Notable sociologists or sociologically influential scholars who won Nobel-type prizes

*   Gunnar Myrdal (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1974): Trained as an economist, Myrdal’s work bridged social policy, institutions, and race—widely cited in social science and sociology.
*   Friedrich Hayek (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1974): Economist by training but engaged with social theory; influential in sociology of knowledge and institutional analysis debates.
*   Amartya Sen (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1998): Economist whose capability approach and work on welfare, development, and social choice have been extensively adopted by sociologists.
*   Douglass North (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1993): Economic historian; his institutional analysis influenced sociological studies of institutions and organizations.
*   Elinor Ostrom (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 2009): Political economist whose work on common-pool resources intersects with sociology, political sociology, and collective action theory.
*   John Hume (Nobel Peace Prize, 1998): Political leader whose work in peace-building has overlap with sociological studies of conflict and social movements.
*   Pope John Paul II (Nobel Peace Prize nominations/discussions, not a laureate): included here as clarification—several prominent sociological figures were influential in peace-related activities though not laureates.

Other relevant laureates with sociological impact

*   Herbert A. Simon (Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, 1978): Work on decision-making, organizations, and bounded rationality is foundational for organizational sociology.
*   Robert Fogel and Douglass North (both economics laureates): Their cliometric and institutional approaches have been used by sociologists studying historical sociology and institutions.

How sociologists are recognized instead

*   Prestigious sociology awards: American Sociological Association (ASA) awards, the Erasmus Prize, Holberg Prize, and various discipline-specific honors are primary recognition venues for sociologists.
*   Interdisciplinary prizes: Many sociologists receive major prizes in economics, political science, or peace-related awards when their work crosses disciplinary boundaries.

Takeaway

*   No Nobel Prize specifically for sociology exists, so no laureate is formally a “Nobel Prize in Sociology” winner. Several Nobel laureates come from neighboring disciplines or produced work that substantially influenced sociology; when sociology crosses into economics, peace studies, or literature, those contributions sometimes earn Nobel recognition.

How Would Biological Immortality Have Changed the Evolution of Life on Earth?

What would have happened if biological immortality had become widespread among animals during the evolutionary history of life on Earth?

Here, biological immortality means the absence of aging and death from age-related decline, not absolute invulnerability: animals could still die from predators, infections, starvation, injuries, and natural disasters.

For an individual organism, death is the end of life. But in the history of evolution, mortality became one of the factors enabling generational turnover and evolutionary renewal. Paradoxically, the finite lifespans of individual organisms helped make life as a process more resilient to change.

Immortality by itself would not have meant unlimited population growth. Yet a major reduction in mortality would have created a fundamental tension between the lifespan of individuals and the limited carrying capacity of the environment.

Each new generation would add individuals to a population already in existence. If birth rates remained high, population size would quickly approach the limits imposed by available food, water, and territory. Crowding, resource shortages, disease, and intraspecific competition would intensify. In this sense, mortality served as one of the natural checks on overpopulation — an excess of life relative to the carrying capacity of the environment.

Under such conditions, reproduction would come under intense pressure. In many species, energy shortages, chronic stress, and high population density reduce reproductive success. If ecological niches and social positions remained occupied by adult individuals for long periods, younger individuals would also find it more difficult to secure territory, resources, and opportunities to reproduce.

In a population of biologically immortal organisms, maintaining a stable population size would require either that new births be balanced by deaths or emigration, or that reproduction be reduced. The spread of immortality under conditions of limited resources would therefore likely be accompanied by the evolution of mechanisms that sharply restrict reproduction.

An especially important consequence would be a slowdown in generational turnover. Evolution depends on heritable variation, mutations, recombination, and differences in reproductive success. New genetic variants arise and spread across generations. The less frequently generations turn over, the more slowly evolutionary renewal generally proceeds.

Immortality would not stop natural selection: as long as differences in survival and reproduction exist, selection continues to operate. But extreme longevity combined with infrequent reproduction would allow established genotypes to persist for much longer and could slow their replacement by new ones. If the climate changed abruptly, a new pathogen emerged, or another ecological catastrophe occurred, such a population might be less capable of rapid evolutionary adaptation.

There is also an ecological dimension. The death of organisms is an important part of the cycling of matter: decomposition returns carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other elements to the ecosystem. With a sharp decline in mortality, a substantial share of these elements would remain bound in living biomass for longer, slowing their return to detrital food webs and soil ecosystems. The cycling of matter would not stop completely, since exchange also occurs while organisms are alive, but the structure of ecosystems would change substantially.

Thus, mortality is deeply embedded in the workings of evolution on Earth. It limits overpopulation, frees ecological space, facilitates generational turnover, and plays a role in the cycling of matter. This does not mean that nature deliberately “invented” death for these purposes. Rather, evolution unfolded in a world of mortal organisms, where generational turnover became one of the most important mechanisms of evolutionary renewal.

Here lies a profound paradox: death ends the life of an individual organism, yet the mortality of organisms has contributed to the continuity, capacity for renewal, and adaptability of life as a whole.

Immortality without intelligence and the ability to regulate reproduction, resources, and the state of ecosystems could therefore become not life’s highest victory, but a source of profound crisis.

But with the emergence of intelligence, a new possibility arises. In blind evolution, renewal occurred through generational turnover and the death of individuals. An intelligent civilization could, in principle, try to replace this mechanism with conscious regulation of reproduction, resources, the environment, and its own biological renewal.

Perhaps the central challenge of the future is to preserve individual life while taking over the regulatory and renewal roles that mortality has played for billions of years.

Jindal Institute of Behavioural Sciences offers students internship opportunities that often lead to employment, especially for those interested in Child Psychology.

The institute mainly focuses on field learning programmes, and hence the students get to work within organisations right from the first semester, where they can directly engage with children, understand their developmental concerns, and help with mental health and wellbeing.

A number of students from the Applied Psychology programme at JIBS have completed their internships with NGOs and social impact organisations such as Child Rights and You (CRY), Bal Raksha Bharat, Pehchan, and India Vision Foundation.

Students inclined towards clinical or therapeutic work also intern at healthcare and rehabilitation centres, including the Institute of Human Behaviour and Allied Sciences, Hopes Autism Centre, and Hope Trust Psychiatric Clinic.

Through these placements, they gain practical experience in psychological assessment, behaviour management, and working closely with children and their families.

In addition, there are opportunities in corporate and organisational sectors where students apply psychological skills such as behavioural analysis, basic counselling, and communication within HR, learning and development, or CSR teams. These types of roles are valuable for those interested in child-focused programmes within larger institutional systems.

Some students also join short-term global programmes offered by JIBS. This could involve visits to schools, community-based institutions, or research facilities.

JIBS offers a range of internship programmes that help Child Psychology students develop effective skill sets in clinical and community settings.

| Number of laureates | 633 prizes awarded to 1,018 individuals and organizations (as of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nobel_Prize&action=edit)) |
| Website | [nobelprize.org](https://www.nobelprize.org/) |

The **Nobel Prizes[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-4)** are awards administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") and granted in accordance with the [principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle "Principle") of "for the greatest benefit to humankind". The prizes were first awarded in 1901, marking the fifth anniversary of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")'s death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-:0-2) The original Nobel Prizes covered five fields: [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"), [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry"), physiology or medicine, [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), and [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), specified in Nobel's will. A sixth prize, the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"), was established in 1968 by [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (Sweden's central bank) in memory of Alfred Nobel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-6) The Nobel Prizes are widely regarded as the most prestigious awards available in their respective fields.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Shalev8-8)

Except in extraordinary circumstances, such as war, all six prizes are given annually. Each recipient, known as a [laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate"), receives a [green gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrum "Electrum")[medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal") plated with [24 karat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_karat "24 karat") gold, a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma"), and a monetary award. As of 2023, the Nobel Prize monetary award is 11,000,000 [kr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), equivalent to approximately US$1,035,000.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-PrizeAmount-3) No more than three individuals may share a prize, although the Nobel Peace Prize can be awarded to organisations of more than three people.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-9) Nobel Prizes are not [awarded posthumously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posthumous_award "Posthumous award"), but if a person is awarded a prize and dies before receiving it, the prize is presented.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-cbc1003-10)

Between 1901 and 2026, the five Nobel Prizes and the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") (since 1969) were awarded 633 times to 1,018 people and organisations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-11) Five individuals and two organisations have received more than one Nobel Prize.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-12)

## History

[![Image 7: A black and white photo of a bearded man in his fifties sitting in a chair.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg/250px-AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg)

One story says that [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel") had the unpleasant surprise of reading his own obituary, which was titled "The Merchant of Death Is Dead", in a French newspaper

[Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel") was born on 21 October 1833 in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), Sweden, into a family of engineers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz5-13) He was a [chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist "Chemist"), [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer"), and [inventor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inventor "Inventor"). In 1894, Nobel purchased the [Bofors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bofors "Bofors") iron and steel mill, which he made into a major [armaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapon "Weapon")[manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing "Manufacturing"). Nobel also invented [ballistite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistite "Ballistite"). This invention was a precursor to many smokeless military explosives, especially the British smokeless powder [cordite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordite "Cordite"). As a consequence of his patent claims, Nobel was eventually involved in a [patent infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement")[lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") over cordite. Nobel amassed a fortune during his lifetime, with most of his wealth coming from his 355 inventions, of which [dynamite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamite "Dynamite") is the most famous.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz11-14)

There is a popular story about how, in 1888, Nobel was astonished to read his own [obituary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obituary "Obituary"), titled "The Merchant of Death Is Dead", in a French newspaper. It was Alfred's brother [Ludvig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludvig_Nobel "Ludvig Nobel") who had died; the [obituary was eight years premature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_premature_obituaries "List of premature obituaries"). The article disconcerted Nobel and made him apprehensive about how he would be remembered. This would have inspired him to change his [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Time-15) Historians have been unable to verify this story and some dismiss the story as a myth.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Smiths-17)

On 10 December 1896, Alfred Nobel died in [his villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Nobel "Villa Nobel") in [San Remo, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo "Sanremo"), from a [cerebral haemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hemorrhage "Cerebral hemorrhage"). He was 63 years old.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Sohlman13-18)

Nobel wrote several wills during his lifetime. He composed the last over a year before he died, signing it at the Swedish–Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Sohlman7-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-20) To widespread astonishment, Nobel's last will specified that his fortune be used to create a series of prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind" in [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"), [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry"), [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") or [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature "Literature"), and [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal1-21) Nobel bequeathed 94% of his total assets, 31 million SEK (c. US$186 million, €150 million in 2008), to establish the five Nobel Prizes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams7-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-NobelFoundationPrizeAmount-23) Owing to skepticism surrounding the will, it was not approved by the [Storting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storting "Storting") in [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") until 26 April 1897.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz13-25-24) The [executors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executors "Executors") of the will, [Ragnar Sohlman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Sohlman "Ragnar Sohlman") and Rudolf Lilljequist, formed the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") to take care of the fortune and to organise the awarding of prizes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams7-8-25)

Nobel's instructions named a [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") to award the [Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), the members of which were appointed shortly after the will was approved in April 1897. Soon thereafter, the other prize-awarding organisations were designated. These were the [Karolinska Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karolinska_Institute "Karolinska Institute") on 7 June, the Swedish Academy on 9 June, and the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") on 11 June.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Crawford1-26) The Nobel Foundation reached an agreement on guidelines for how the prizes should be awarded; and, in 1900, the Nobel Foundation's newly created [statutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute "Statute") were promulgated by [King Oscar II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_II_of_Sweden "Oscar II of Sweden").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal1-21)

### Nobel Foundation

#### Formation of Nobel Foundation

Main article: [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation")

[![Image 8: A paper with stylish handwriting on it with the title "Testament"](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th%2C_1895.jpg/250px-Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th%2C_1895.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th,_1895.jpg)

Alfred Nobel's [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament"), which stated that 94% of his total assets should be used to establish the Nobel Prizes

According to his will and testament read in Stockholm on 30 December 1896, a foundation established by Alfred Nobel would reward those who serve humanity. The Nobel Prize was funded by Alfred Nobel's personal fortune. According to the official sources, Alfred Nobel bequeathed most of his fortune to the Nobel Foundation that now forms the economic base of the Nobel Prize.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-27)

The [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") was founded as a private organisation on 29 June 1900. Its function is to manage the finances and administration of the Nobel Prizes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz14-28) In accordance with Nobel's [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament"), the primary task of the foundation is to manage the fortune left to posterity by Nobel. [Robert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Nobel "Robert Nobel") and [Ludvig Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludvig_Nobel "Ludvig Nobel") were involved in the [oil business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_business "Oil business") in [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), and according to Swedish [historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historian "Historian") E. Bargengren, who accessed the [Nobel family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_family "Nobel family")[archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archive "Archive"), it was this "decision to allow withdrawal of Alfred's money from [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku") that became the decisive factor that enabled the Nobel Prizes to be established".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-29) Another important task of the Nobel Foundation is to market the prizes internationally and to oversee informal administration related to the prizes. The foundation is not involved in the process of selecting the [Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_laureates "Nobel laureates").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-31) In many ways, the Nobel Foundation is similar to an [investment company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_company "Investment company"), in that it invests Nobel's money to create a solid funding base for the prizes and the administrative activities. The Nobel Foundation is [exempt from all taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_exemption "Tax exemption") in Sweden (since 1946) and from investment taxes in the United States (since 1953).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz17-18-32) Since the 1980s, the foundation's investments have become more profitable and as of 31 December 2007, the assets controlled by the Nobel Foundation amounted to 3.628 billion Swedish _kronor_ (c. US $560 million).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-17-33)

According to the statutes, the foundation consists of a board of five Swedish or Norwegian citizens, with its seat in Stockholm. The [chairman of the board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_board "Chairman of the board") is appointed by the Swedish [King in Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Sweden "Privy Council of Sweden"), with the other four members appointed by the [trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustee "Trustee") of the prize-awarding institutions. An [executive director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_director "Executive director") is chosen from among the [board members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors"), a deputy director is appointed by the King in Council, and two deputies are appointed by the [trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustees "Trustees"). However, since 1995, all the members of the board have been chosen by the trustees, and the executive director and the deputy director appointed by the board itself. As well as the board, the Nobel Foundation is made up of the prize-awarding institutions (the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute, the Swedish Academy, and the [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee")), the trustees of these institutions, and [auditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audit "Audit").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-17-33)

#### Foundation capital and cost

The capital of the Nobel Foundation today is invested 50% in [shares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Share_capital "Share capital"), 20% [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_(finance) "Bond (finance)") and 30% other [investments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investments "Investments") (e.g. [hedge funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_funds "Hedge funds") or [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate")). The distribution can vary by 10 percent.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-dn20121202-34) At the beginning of 2008, 64% of the funds were invested mainly in American and European stocks, 20% in bonds, plus 12% in real estate and hedge funds.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-handelsblatt2008-35)

In 2011, the total annual cost was approximately 120 million [kronor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), with 50 million kronor as the prize money. Further costs to pay institutions and persons engaged in giving the prizes were 27.4 million kronor. The events during the Nobel week in Stockholm and Oslo cost 20.2 million kronor. The administration, Nobel [symposium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_conference "Academic conference"), and similar items had costs of 22.4 million kronor. The cost of the [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") prize of 16.5 Million kronor is paid by the [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-dn20121202-34)

### Inaugural Nobel prizes

[![Image 9: A black and white photo of a bearded man in his fifties sitting in a chair.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/R%C3%B6ntgen%2C_Wilhelm_Conrad_%281845-1923%29.jpg/250px-R%C3%B6ntgen%2C_Wilhelm_Conrad_%281845-1923%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:R%C3%B6ntgen,_Wilhelm_Conrad_(1845-1923).jpg)

[Wilhelm Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen"), who received the first [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") for his discovery of the [X-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray")

Once the Nobel Foundation and its guidelines were in place, the [Nobel Committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Committee "Nobel Committee") began collecting nominations for the inaugural prizes. Subsequently, they sent a list of preliminary candidates to the prize-awarding institutions.

The Nobel Committee's Physics Prize shortlist cited [Wilhelm Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen")'s discovery of [X-rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") and [Philipp Lenard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipp_Lenard "Philipp Lenard")'s work on [cathode rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode_ray "Cathode ray"). The Academy of Sciences selected Röntgen for the prize.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman134-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Leroy117-118-37) In the last decades of the 19th century, many chemists had made significant contributions. Thus, with the Chemistry Prize, the academy "was chiefly faced with merely deciding the order in which these scientists should be awarded the prize".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz77-38) The academy received 20 nominations, eleven of them for [Jacobus van 't Hoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobus_Henricus_van_'t_Hoff "Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Crawford118-39) Van 't Hoff was awarded the prize for his contributions in [chemical thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_thermodynamics "Chemical thermodynamics").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz81-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman205-41)

The Swedish Academy chose the poet [Sully Prudhomme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sully_Prudhomme "Sully Prudhomme") for the first Nobel Prize in Literature. A group including 42 Swedish writers, artists, and literary critics protested against this decision, having expected [Leo Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy") to be awarded.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz144-42) Some, including [Burton Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burton_Feldman "Burton Feldman"), have criticised this prize because they consider Prudhomme a mediocre poet. Feldman's explanation is that most of the academy members preferred [Victorian literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_literature "Victorian literature") and thus selected a Victorian poet.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman69-43) The first Physiology or Medicine Prize went to the German physiologist and microbiologist [Emil von Behring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_von_Behring "Emil von Behring"). During the 1890s, von Behring developed an [antitoxin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitoxin "Antitoxin") to treat [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria"), which until then had been causing thousands of deaths each year.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman242-244-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Leroy233-45)

The first [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") went to the Swiss [Jean Henri Dunant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Dunant "Henry Dunant") for his role in founding the International [Red Cross Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement") and initiating the Geneva Convention, and jointly given to French pacifist [Frédéric Passy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Passy "Frédéric Passy"), founder of the Peace League and active with Dunant in the Alliance for Order and Civilization.

### Second World War

In 1938 and 1939, [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s [Third Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") forbade three laureates from Germany ([Richard Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn"), [Adolf Friedrich Johann Butenandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt"), and [Gerhard Domagk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk")) from accepting their prizes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz23-46) They were all later able to receive the diploma and medal.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Wilhelm85-47) Even though Sweden was officially neutral during the Second World War, the prizes were awarded irregularly. In 1939, the Peace Prize was not awarded. No prize was awarded in any category from 1940 to 1942, due to the [occupation of Norway by Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_occupation_of_Norway "German occupation of Norway"). In the subsequent year, all prizes were awarded except those for literature and peace.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-48)

During the occupation of Norway, three members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee fled into exile. The remaining members escaped persecution from the Germans when the Nobel Foundation stated that the committee building in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") was Swedish property. Thus it was a safe haven from the German military, which was not at war with Sweden.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams23-49) These members kept the work of the committee going, but did not award any prizes. In 1944, the Nobel Foundation, together with the three members in exile, made sure that nominations were submitted for the Peace Prize and that the prize could be awarded once again.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz23-46)

### Prize in Economic Sciences

Main article: [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG/250px-Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG)

Map of Nobel laureates by country

After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") evolved rapidly as an academic discipline and came to be increasingly recognized as a significant scientific field.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-50) In 1968, Sweden's central bank, [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank"), celebrated its 300th anniversary and donated a sum of money to the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") to be used to set up a new award in the field of [economic sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_sciences "Economic sciences"). The following year, 1969, the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") was awarded for the first time. [The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") is required to select the economics laureate in the same way as it does for the science Nobel Prizes. The first laureates for the Economics Prize were [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen") and [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch"), "for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman343-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz207-52) The board of the Nobel Foundation decided that after this addition, it would allow no further new prizes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz20-53)

## Award process

The award process is similar for all of the Nobel Prizes, the main difference being who can make nominations for each of them.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-17-54)

### Nominations

Nomination forms are sent by the Nobel Committee to about 3,000 individuals, usually in September the year before the prizes are awarded. These individuals are generally prominent academics working in a relevant area. Regarding the Peace Prize, inquiries are also sent to governments, former Peace Prize laureates, and current or former members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. The deadline for the return of the nomination forms is 31 January of the year of the award.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-17-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz26-55) The Nobel Committee nominates about 300 potential laureates from these forms and additional names.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams15-56) The nominees are not publicly named, nor are they told that they are being considered for the prize. All nomination records for a prize are sealed for 50 years from the awarding of the prize.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman315-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-58)

Main article: [List of Nobel laureates §50-year secrecy rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#50-year_secrecy_rule "List of Nobel laureates")

### Selection

The Nobel Committee then prepares a report reflecting the advice of experts in the relevant fields. This, along with the list of preliminary candidates, is submitted to the prize-awarding institutions.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman52-59) There are four awarding institutions for the six prizes awarded:

*   [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") – Chemistry; Physics; Economics
*   [Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Assembly_at_the_Karolinska_Institute "Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute") – Physiology / Medicine
*   [Swedish Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Academy "Swedish Academy") – Literature
*   [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") – Peace

The institutions meet to choose the laureate or laureates in each field by a majority vote. Their decision, which cannot be appealed, is announced immediately after the vote.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz25-28-60) A maximum of three laureates and two different works may be selected per award. Except for the Peace Prize, which can be awarded to institutions, the awards can only be given to individuals.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams8-61) The winners are announced by the awarding institutions during the first two weeks of October.

### Posthumous nominations

Although posthumous nominations are not presently permitted, individuals who died in the months between their nomination and the decision of the prize committee were originally eligible to receive the prize.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-62) This has occurred twice: the 1931 Literature Prize awarded to [Erik Axel Karlfeldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Axel_Karlfeldt "Erik Axel Karlfeldt"), and the 1961 Peace Prize awarded to [UN Secretary General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations")[Dag Hammarskjöld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dag_Hammarskj%C3%B6ld "Dag Hammarskjöld"). Since 1974, laureates must be thought alive at the time of the October announcement. There has been one laureate, [William Vickrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Vickrey "William Vickrey"), who in 1996 died after the prize (in [Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences")) was announced but before it could be presented.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams9-63) On 3 October 2011, the laureates for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine were announced; however, the committee was not aware that one of the laureates, [Ralph M. Steinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_M._Steinman "Ralph M. Steinman"), had died three days earlier. The committee reconsidered Steinman's award, since the rule is that the prize is not awarded posthumously,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-cbc1003-10) but decided that as the decision to award Steinman the prize "was made in good faith", it would remain unchanged, and the prize would be awarded.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-64)

### Recognition time lag

Nobel's will provided for prizes to be awarded in recognition of discoveries made "during the preceding year". Early on, the awards usually recognised recent discoveries.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-65) However, some of those early discoveries were later discredited. For example, [Johannes Fibiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Fibiger "Johannes Fibiger") was awarded the 1926 Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his purported discovery of a parasite that caused cancer.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz125-66) To avoid repeating this embarrassment, the awards increasingly recognised scientific discoveries that had withstood the test of time.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams25-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-embo-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-scienceline1-69) According to Ralf Pettersson, former chairman of the Nobel Prize Committee for Physiology or Medicine, "the criterion 'the previous year' is interpreted by the Nobel Assembly as the year when the full impact of the discovery has become evident."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-embo-68)

[![Image 11: A room with pictures on the walls. In the middle of the room there is a wooden table with chairs around it.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg/250px-Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg)

The committee room of the Norwegian Nobel Committee

The interval between the award and the accomplishment it recognises varies from discipline to discipline. The Literature Prize is typically awarded to recognise a cumulative lifetime body of work rather than a single achievement.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-71) The Peace Prize can also be awarded for a lifetime body of work. For example, 2008 laureate [Martti Ahtisaari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martti_Ahtisaari "Martti Ahtisaari") was awarded for his work to resolve international conflicts.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-73) However, they can also be awarded for specific recent events.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-74) For instance, [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan") was awarded the 2001 Peace Prize just four years after becoming the Secretary-General of the United Nations.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams330-75) Similarly [Yasser Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat "Yasser Arafat"), [Yitzhak Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Rabin "Yitzhak Rabin"), and [Shimon Peres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimon_Peres "Shimon Peres") received the 1994 award, about a year after they successfully concluded the [Oslo Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Accords "Oslo Accords").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams27-76) A [controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_controversies "Nobel Prize controversies") was caused by awarding the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize to [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") during his first year as US president.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-78)

Awards for physics, chemistry, and medicine are typically awarded once the achievement has been widely accepted. Sometimes, this takes decades – for example, [Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subrahmanyan_Chandrasekhar "Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar") shared the 1983 Physics Prize for his 1930s work on stellar structure and evolution.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-currentscience-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-80) Not all scientists live long enough for their work to be recognised. Some discoveries can never be considered for a prize if their impact is realised after the discoverers have died.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-83)
