The **Nobel Prizes[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-4)** are awards administered by the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") and granted in accordance with the [principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle "Principle") of "for the greatest benefit to humankind". The prizes were first awarded in 1901, marking the fifth anniversary of [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel")'s death.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-:0-2) The original Nobel Prizes covered five fields: [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics"), [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry "Nobel Prize in Chemistry"), physiology or medicine, [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "Nobel Prize in Literature"), and [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), specified in Nobel's will. A sixth prize, the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"), was established in 1968 by [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank") (Sweden's central bank) in memory of Alfred Nobel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-6) The Nobel Prizes are widely regarded as the most prestigious awards available in their respective fields.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Shalev8-8)

Except in extraordinary circumstances, such as war, all six prizes are given annually. Each recipient, known as a [laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureate "Laureate"), receives a [green gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrum "Electrum")[medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal") plated with [24 karat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_karat "24 karat") gold, a [diploma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diploma "Diploma"), and a monetary award. As of 2023, the Nobel Prize monetary award is 11,000,000 [kr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), equivalent to approximately US$1,035,000.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-PrizeAmount-3) No more than three individuals may share a prize, although the Nobel Peace Prize can be awarded to organisations of more than three people.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-9) Nobel Prizes are not [awarded posthumously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posthumous_award "Posthumous award"), but if a person is awarded a prize and dies before receiving it, the prize is presented.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-cbc1003-10)

Between 1901 and 2026, the five Nobel Prizes and the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") (since 1969) were awarded 633 times to 1,018 people and organisations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-11) Five individuals and two organisations have received more than one Nobel Prize.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-12)

## History

[![Image 7: A black and white photo of a bearded man in his fifties sitting in a chair.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg/250px-AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AlfredNobel_adjusted.jpg)

One story says that [Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel") had the unpleasant surprise of reading his own obituary, which was titled "The Merchant of Death Is Dead", in a French newspaper

[Alfred Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Nobel "Alfred Nobel") was born on 21 October 1833 in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), Sweden, into a family of engineers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz5-13) He was a [chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist "Chemist"), [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer"), and [inventor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inventor "Inventor"). In 1894, Nobel purchased the [Bofors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bofors "Bofors") iron and steel mill, which he made into a major [armaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapon "Weapon")[manufacturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manufacturing "Manufacturing"). Nobel also invented [ballistite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistite "Ballistite"). This invention was a precursor to many smokeless military explosives, especially the British smokeless powder [cordite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordite "Cordite"). As a consequence of his patent claims, Nobel was eventually involved in a [patent infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patent_infringement "Patent infringement")[lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit "Lawsuit") over cordite. Nobel amassed a fortune during his lifetime, with most of his wealth coming from his 355 inventions, of which [dynamite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamite "Dynamite") is the most famous.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz11-14)

There is a popular story about how, in 1888, Nobel was astonished to read his own [obituary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obituary "Obituary"), titled "The Merchant of Death Is Dead", in a French newspaper. It was Alfred's brother [Ludvig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludvig_Nobel "Ludvig Nobel") who had died; the [obituary was eight years premature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_premature_obituaries "List of premature obituaries"). The article disconcerted Nobel and made him apprehensive about how he would be remembered. This would have inspired him to change his [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Time-15) Historians have been unable to verify this story and some dismiss the story as a myth.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Smiths-17)

On 10 December 1896, Alfred Nobel died in [his villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Nobel "Villa Nobel") in [San Remo, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo "Sanremo"), from a [cerebral haemorrhage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_hemorrhage "Cerebral hemorrhage"). He was 63 years old.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Sohlman13-18)

Nobel wrote several wills during his lifetime. He composed the last over a year before he died, signing it at the Swedish–Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Sohlman7-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-20) To widespread astonishment, Nobel's last will specified that his fortune be used to create a series of prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind" in [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"), [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry"), [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology") or [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature "Literature"), and [peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace "Peace").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal1-21) Nobel bequeathed 94% of his total assets, 31 million SEK (c. US$186 million, €150 million in 2008), to establish the five Nobel Prizes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams7-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-NobelFoundationPrizeAmount-23) Owing to skepticism surrounding the will, it was not approved by the [Storting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storting "Storting") in [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") until 26 April 1897.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz13-25-24) The [executors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executors "Executors") of the will, [Ragnar Sohlman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Sohlman "Ragnar Sohlman") and Rudolf Lilljequist, formed the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") to take care of the fortune and to organise the awarding of prizes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams7-8-25)

Nobel's instructions named a [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") to award the [Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize"), the members of which were appointed shortly after the will was approved in April 1897. Soon thereafter, the other prize-awarding organisations were designated. These were the [Karolinska Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karolinska_Institute "Karolinska Institute") on 7 June, the Swedish Academy on 9 June, and the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") on 11 June.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Crawford1-26) The Nobel Foundation reached an agreement on guidelines for how the prizes should be awarded; and, in 1900, the Nobel Foundation's newly created [statutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute "Statute") were promulgated by [King Oscar II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_II_of_Sweden "Oscar II of Sweden").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal1-21)

### Nobel Foundation

#### Formation of Nobel Foundation

Main article: [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation")

[![Image 8: A paper with stylish handwriting on it with the title "Testament"](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th%2C_1895.jpg/250px-Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th%2C_1895.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alfred_Nobels_will-November_25th,_1895.jpg)

Alfred Nobel's [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament"), which stated that 94% of his total assets should be used to establish the Nobel Prizes

According to his will and testament read in Stockholm on 30 December 1896, a foundation established by Alfred Nobel would reward those who serve humanity. The Nobel Prize was funded by Alfred Nobel's personal fortune. According to the official sources, Alfred Nobel bequeathed most of his fortune to the Nobel Foundation that now forms the economic base of the Nobel Prize.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-27)

The [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") was founded as a private organisation on 29 June 1900. Its function is to manage the finances and administration of the Nobel Prizes.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz14-28) In accordance with Nobel's [will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_and_testament "Will and testament"), the primary task of the foundation is to manage the fortune left to posterity by Nobel. [Robert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Nobel "Robert Nobel") and [Ludvig Nobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludvig_Nobel "Ludvig Nobel") were involved in the [oil business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_business "Oil business") in [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan"), and according to Swedish [historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historian "Historian") E. Bargengren, who accessed the [Nobel family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_family "Nobel family")[archive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archive "Archive"), it was this "decision to allow withdrawal of Alfred's money from [Baku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baku "Baku") that became the decisive factor that enabled the Nobel Prizes to be established".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-29) Another important task of the Nobel Foundation is to market the prizes internationally and to oversee informal administration related to the prizes. The foundation is not involved in the process of selecting the [Nobel laureates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_laureates "Nobel laureates").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-31) In many ways, the Nobel Foundation is similar to an [investment company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_company "Investment company"), in that it invests Nobel's money to create a solid funding base for the prizes and the administrative activities. The Nobel Foundation is [exempt from all taxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_exemption "Tax exemption") in Sweden (since 1946) and from investment taxes in the United States (since 1953).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz17-18-32) Since the 1980s, the foundation's investments have become more profitable and as of 31 December 2007, the assets controlled by the Nobel Foundation amounted to 3.628 billion Swedish _kronor_ (c. US $560 million).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-17-33)

According to the statutes, the foundation consists of a board of five Swedish or Norwegian citizens, with its seat in Stockholm. The [chairman of the board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_board "Chairman of the board") is appointed by the Swedish [King in Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_Sweden "Privy Council of Sweden"), with the other four members appointed by the [trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustee "Trustee") of the prize-awarding institutions. An [executive director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_director "Executive director") is chosen from among the [board members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors"), a deputy director is appointed by the King in Council, and two deputies are appointed by the [trustees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustees "Trustees"). However, since 1995, all the members of the board have been chosen by the trustees, and the executive director and the deputy director appointed by the board itself. As well as the board, the Nobel Foundation is made up of the prize-awarding institutions (the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute, the Swedish Academy, and the [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee")), the trustees of these institutions, and [auditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audit "Audit").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz15-17-33)

#### Foundation capital and cost

The capital of the Nobel Foundation today is invested 50% in [shares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Share_capital "Share capital"), 20% [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_(finance) "Bond (finance)") and 30% other [investments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investments "Investments") (e.g. [hedge funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_funds "Hedge funds") or [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate")). The distribution can vary by 10 percent.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-dn20121202-34) At the beginning of 2008, 64% of the funds were invested mainly in American and European stocks, 20% in bonds, plus 12% in real estate and hedge funds.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-handelsblatt2008-35)

In 2011, the total annual cost was approximately 120 million [kronor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"), with 50 million kronor as the prize money. Further costs to pay institutions and persons engaged in giving the prizes were 27.4 million kronor. The events during the Nobel week in Stockholm and Oslo cost 20.2 million kronor. The administration, Nobel [symposium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_conference "Academic conference"), and similar items had costs of 22.4 million kronor. The cost of the [Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Sciences "Economic Sciences") prize of 16.5 Million kronor is paid by the [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-dn20121202-34)

### Inaugural Nobel prizes

[![Image 9: A black and white photo of a bearded man in his fifties sitting in a chair.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/R%C3%B6ntgen%2C_Wilhelm_Conrad_%281845-1923%29.jpg/250px-R%C3%B6ntgen%2C_Wilhelm_Conrad_%281845-1923%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:R%C3%B6ntgen,_Wilhelm_Conrad_(1845-1923).jpg)

[Wilhelm Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen"), who received the first [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") for his discovery of the [X-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray")

Once the Nobel Foundation and its guidelines were in place, the [Nobel Committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Committee "Nobel Committee") began collecting nominations for the inaugural prizes. Subsequently, they sent a list of preliminary candidates to the prize-awarding institutions.

The Nobel Committee's Physics Prize shortlist cited [Wilhelm Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen")'s discovery of [X-rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray "X-ray") and [Philipp Lenard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipp_Lenard "Philipp Lenard")'s work on [cathode rays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathode_ray "Cathode ray"). The Academy of Sciences selected Röntgen for the prize.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman134-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Leroy117-118-37) In the last decades of the 19th century, many chemists had made significant contributions. Thus, with the Chemistry Prize, the academy "was chiefly faced with merely deciding the order in which these scientists should be awarded the prize".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz77-38) The academy received 20 nominations, eleven of them for [Jacobus van 't Hoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobus_Henricus_van_'t_Hoff "Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Crawford118-39) Van 't Hoff was awarded the prize for his contributions in [chemical thermodynamics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_thermodynamics "Chemical thermodynamics").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz81-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman205-41)

The Swedish Academy chose the poet [Sully Prudhomme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sully_Prudhomme "Sully Prudhomme") for the first Nobel Prize in Literature. A group including 42 Swedish writers, artists, and literary critics protested against this decision, having expected [Leo Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy") to be awarded.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz144-42) Some, including [Burton Feldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burton_Feldman "Burton Feldman"), have criticised this prize because they consider Prudhomme a mediocre poet. Feldman's explanation is that most of the academy members preferred [Victorian literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_literature "Victorian literature") and thus selected a Victorian poet.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman69-43) The first Physiology or Medicine Prize went to the German physiologist and microbiologist [Emil von Behring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emil_von_Behring "Emil von Behring"). During the 1890s, von Behring developed an [antitoxin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitoxin "Antitoxin") to treat [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria "Diphtheria"), which until then had been causing thousands of deaths each year.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman242-244-44)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Leroy233-45)

The first [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") went to the Swiss [Jean Henri Dunant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Dunant "Henry Dunant") for his role in founding the International [Red Cross Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement") and initiating the Geneva Convention, and jointly given to French pacifist [Frédéric Passy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Passy "Frédéric Passy"), founder of the Peace League and active with Dunant in the Alliance for Order and Civilization.

### Second World War

In 1938 and 1939, [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler")'s [Third Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") forbade three laureates from Germany ([Richard Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kuhn "Richard Kuhn"), [Adolf Friedrich Johann Butenandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Butenandt "Adolf Butenandt"), and [Gerhard Domagk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Domagk "Gerhard Domagk")) from accepting their prizes.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz23-46) They were all later able to receive the diploma and medal.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Wilhelm85-47) Even though Sweden was officially neutral during the Second World War, the prizes were awarded irregularly. In 1939, the Peace Prize was not awarded. No prize was awarded in any category from 1940 to 1942, due to the [occupation of Norway by Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_occupation_of_Norway "German occupation of Norway"). In the subsequent year, all prizes were awarded except those for literature and peace.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-48)

During the occupation of Norway, three members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee fled into exile. The remaining members escaped persecution from the Germans when the Nobel Foundation stated that the committee building in [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") was Swedish property. Thus it was a safe haven from the German military, which was not at war with Sweden.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams23-49) These members kept the work of the committee going, but did not award any prizes. In 1944, the Nobel Foundation, together with the three members in exile, made sure that nominations were submitted for the Peace Prize and that the prize could be awarded once again.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz23-46)

### Prize in Economic Sciences

Main article: [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG/250px-Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Worldmapnobellaureatesbycountry2.PNG)

Map of Nobel laureates by country

After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") evolved rapidly as an academic discipline and came to be increasingly recognized as a significant scientific field.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-50) In 1968, Sweden's central bank, [Sveriges Riksbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Riksbank "Sveriges Riksbank"), celebrated its 300th anniversary and donated a sum of money to the [Nobel Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Foundation "Nobel Foundation") to be used to set up a new award in the field of [economic sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_sciences "Economic sciences"). The following year, 1969, the [Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") was awarded for the first time. [The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") is required to select the economics laureate in the same way as it does for the science Nobel Prizes. The first laureates for the Economics Prize were [Jan Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen") and [Ragnar Frisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragnar_Frisch "Ragnar Frisch"), "for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman343-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz207-52) The board of the Nobel Foundation decided that after this addition, it would allow no further new prizes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz20-53)

## Award process

The award process is similar for all of the Nobel Prizes, the main difference being who can make nominations for each of them.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-17-54)

### Nominations

Nomination forms are sent by the Nobel Committee to about 3,000 individuals, usually in September the year before the prizes are awarded. These individuals are generally prominent academics working in a relevant area. Regarding the Peace Prize, inquiries are also sent to governments, former Peace Prize laureates, and current or former members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. The deadline for the return of the nomination forms is 31 January of the year of the award.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman16-17-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz26-55) The Nobel Committee nominates about 300 potential laureates from these forms and additional names.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams15-56) The nominees are not publicly named, nor are they told that they are being considered for the prize. All nomination records for a prize are sealed for 50 years from the awarding of the prize.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman315-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-58)

Main article: [List of Nobel laureates §50-year secrecy rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates#50-year_secrecy_rule "List of Nobel laureates")

### Selection

The Nobel Committee then prepares a report reflecting the advice of experts in the relevant fields. This, along with the list of preliminary candidates, is submitted to the prize-awarding institutions.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman52-59) There are four awarding institutions for the six prizes awarded:

*   [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") – Chemistry; Physics; Economics
*   [Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Assembly_at_the_Karolinska_Institute "Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute") – Physiology / Medicine
*   [Swedish Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Academy "Swedish Academy") – Literature
*   [Norwegian Nobel Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Committee "Norwegian Nobel Committee") – Peace

The institutions meet to choose the laureate or laureates in each field by a majority vote. Their decision, which cannot be appealed, is announced immediately after the vote.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz25-28-60) A maximum of three laureates and two different works may be selected per award. Except for the Peace Prize, which can be awarded to institutions, the awards can only be given to individuals.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams8-61) The winners are announced by the awarding institutions during the first two weeks of October.

### Posthumous nominations

Although posthumous nominations are not presently permitted, individuals who died in the months between their nomination and the decision of the prize committee were originally eligible to receive the prize.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-62) This has occurred twice: the 1931 Literature Prize awarded to [Erik Axel Karlfeldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Axel_Karlfeldt "Erik Axel Karlfeldt"), and the 1961 Peace Prize awarded to [UN Secretary General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary-General_of_the_United_Nations "Secretary-General of the United Nations")[Dag Hammarskjöld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dag_Hammarskj%C3%B6ld "Dag Hammarskjöld"). Since 1974, laureates must be thought alive at the time of the October announcement. There has been one laureate, [William Vickrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Vickrey "William Vickrey"), who in 1996 died after the prize (in [Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences")) was announced but before it could be presented.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams9-63) On 3 October 2011, the laureates for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine were announced; however, the committee was not aware that one of the laureates, [Ralph M. Steinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_M._Steinman "Ralph M. Steinman"), had died three days earlier. The committee reconsidered Steinman's award, since the rule is that the prize is not awarded posthumously,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-cbc1003-10) but decided that as the decision to award Steinman the prize "was made in good faith", it would remain unchanged, and the prize would be awarded.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-64)

### Recognition time lag

Nobel's will provided for prizes to be awarded in recognition of discoveries made "during the preceding year". Early on, the awards usually recognised recent discoveries.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-65) However, some of those early discoveries were later discredited. For example, [Johannes Fibiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Fibiger "Johannes Fibiger") was awarded the 1926 Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his purported discovery of a parasite that caused cancer.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz125-66) To avoid repeating this embarrassment, the awards increasingly recognised scientific discoveries that had withstood the test of time.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams25-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-embo-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-scienceline1-69) According to Ralf Pettersson, former chairman of the Nobel Prize Committee for Physiology or Medicine, "the criterion 'the previous year' is interpreted by the Nobel Assembly as the year when the full impact of the discovery has become evident."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-embo-68)

[![Image 11: A room with pictures on the walls. In the middle of the room there is a wooden table with chairs around it.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg/250px-Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobelinstituttet_20080913-01.jpg)

The committee room of the Norwegian Nobel Committee

The interval between the award and the accomplishment it recognises varies from discipline to discipline. The Literature Prize is typically awarded to recognise a cumulative lifetime body of work rather than a single achievement.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-71) The Peace Prize can also be awarded for a lifetime body of work. For example, 2008 laureate [Martti Ahtisaari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martti_Ahtisaari "Martti Ahtisaari") was awarded for his work to resolve international conflicts.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-73) However, they can also be awarded for specific recent events.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-74) For instance, [Kofi Annan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Annan "Kofi Annan") was awarded the 2001 Peace Prize just four years after becoming the Secretary-General of the United Nations.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams330-75) Similarly [Yasser Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat "Yasser Arafat"), [Yitzhak Rabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yitzhak_Rabin "Yitzhak Rabin"), and [Shimon Peres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimon_Peres "Shimon Peres") received the 1994 award, about a year after they successfully concluded the [Oslo Accords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_Accords "Oslo Accords").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams27-76) A [controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_controversies "Nobel Prize controversies") was caused by awarding the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize to [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") during his first year as US president.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-78)

Awards for physics, chemistry, and medicine are typically awarded once the achievement has been widely accepted. Sometimes, this takes decades – for example, [Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subrahmanyan_Chandrasekhar "Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar") shared the 1983 Physics Prize for his 1930s work on stellar structure and evolution.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-currentscience-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-80) Not all scientists live long enough for their work to be recognised. Some discoveries can never be considered for a prize if their impact is realised after the discoverers have died.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-83)

Except for the Peace Prize, the Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm, Sweden, at the annual Prize Award Ceremony on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death. The recipients' lectures are normally held in the days prior to the award ceremony. The Peace Prize and its recipients' lectures are presented at the annual Prize Award Ceremony in Oslo, Norway, usually on 10 December. The award ceremonies and the associated banquets are typically major international events.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-autogenerated5-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal2-85) The Prizes awarded in Sweden's ceremonies are held at the [Stockholm Concert Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_Concert_Hall "Stockholm Concert Hall"), with the Nobel banquet following immediately at [Stockholm City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_City_Hall "Stockholm City Hall"). The Nobel Peace Prize ceremony has been held at the [Norwegian Nobel Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Nobel_Institute "Norwegian Nobel Institute") (1905–1946), at the [auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditorium "Auditorium") of the [University of Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oslo "University of Oslo") (1947–1989), and at [Oslo City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo_City_Hall "Oslo City Hall") (1990–present).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Levinovitz21-23-86)

The highlight of the Nobel Prize Award Ceremony in Stockholm occurs when each Nobel laureate steps forward to receive the prize from the hands of the [King of Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Sweden "Monarchy of Sweden"). In Oslo, the chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee presents the Nobel Peace Prize in the presence of the [King of Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarchy_of_Norway "Monarchy of Norway") and the [Norwegian royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_royal_family "Norwegian royal family").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-thelocal2-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-sweden2-87) At first, King [Oscar II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_II_of_Sweden "Oscar II of Sweden") did not approve of awarding grand prizes to foreigners.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-88)

### Nobel Banquet

Main article: [Nobel Banquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Banquet "Nobel Banquet")

[![Image 14: A set table with a white table cloth. There are many plates and glasses plus a menu visible on the table.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Nobel-banquet-table.jpg/250px-Nobel-banquet-table.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel-banquet-table.jpg)

Table at the 2005 [Nobel Banquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Banquet "Nobel Banquet") in Stockholm

After the award ceremony in Sweden, a banquet is held in the [Blue Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Hall "Blue Hall") at the [Stockholm City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_City_Hall "Stockholm City Hall"), which is attended by the [Swedish Royal Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Royal_Family "Swedish Royal Family") and around 1,300 guests. The [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") banquet is held in Norway at the [Oslo Grand Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Hotel_(Oslo) "Grand Hotel (Oslo)") after the award ceremony. Apart from the laureate, guests include the president of the [Storting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storting "Storting"), on occasion the Swedish prime minister, and, since 2006, the King and Queen of Norway. In total, about 250 guests attend.

### Nobel lecture

According to the statutes of the Nobel Foundation, each laureate is required to give a public lecture on a subject related to the topic of their prize.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-89) The Nobel lecture as a rhetorical genre took decades to reach its current format.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-90) These lectures normally occur during Nobel Week (the week leading up to the award ceremony and banquet, which begins with the laureates arriving in Stockholm and normally ends with the Nobel banquet), but this is not mandatory. The laureate is only obliged to give the lecture within six months of receiving the prize, but some have happened even later. For example, US President [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") received the Peace Prize in 1906 but gave his lecture in 1910, after his term in office.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams18-19-91) The lectures are organised by the same association which selected the laureates.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-92)

### Nobel Minds

From 1959 to 1990, Swedish journalist [Bengt Feldreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengt_Feldreich "Bengt Feldreich") gathered the science prize laureates to a discussion, broadcast as _Snillen spekulerar_ (in English _Science and Man_) first in radio, and then from the mid-1960s in [Sveriges Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sveriges_Television "Sveriges Television"). Since 2004, the program is a coproduction with [BBC World News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_World_News "BBC World News") under the title _Nobel Minds_, since 2011 hosted by [Zeinab Badawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeinab_Badawi "Zeinab Badawi").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-95)

## Prizes

### Medals

Main article: [Nobel Prize medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_medal "Nobel Prize medal")

[![Image 15: A heavily decorated paper with the name "Fritz Haber" on it.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Nobel_Prize_Diploma_Fritz_Haber_1918.JPG/250px-Nobel_Prize_Diploma_Fritz_Haber_1918.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel_Prize_Diploma_Fritz_Haber_1918.JPG)

[Fritz Haber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Haber "Fritz Haber")'s diploma is shown, which he received for the development of a method to synthesise [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia"). Laureates receive a heavily decorated diploma together with a gold medal and prize money

The Nobel Foundation announced on 30 May 2012 that it had awarded the contract for the production of the five (Swedish) Nobel Prize medals to Svenska Medalj AB. Between 1902 and 2010, the Nobel Prize medals were minted by [Myntverket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myntverket "Myntverket") (the Swedish Mint), which ceased operations in 2011 after 107 years. In 2011, the Mint of Norway, located in Kongsberg, made the medals. The Nobel Prize medals are registered trademarks of the Nobel Foundation.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-96)

Each medal features an image of Alfred Nobel in left profile on the [obverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obverse_and_reverse "Obverse and reverse"). The medals for physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, and literature have identical obverses, showing the image of Alfred Nobel and the years of his birth and death. Nobel's portrait also appears on the obverse of the Peace Prize medal and the medal for the Economics Prize, but with a slightly different design. For instance, the laureate's name is engraved on the rim of the Economics medal.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman2-97) The image on the reverse of a medal varies according to the institution awarding the prize. The reverse sides of the medals for chemistry and physics share the same design.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Paulingmedal-98)

All medals made before 1980 were struck in 23 [carat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carat_(purity) "Carat (purity)") gold. Since then, they have been struck in 18 carat [green gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured_gold#Green_gold "Coloured gold") plated with 24 carat gold. The weight of each medal varies with the value of gold, but averages about 175 grams (0.386 lb) for each medal. The diameter is 66 millimetres (2.6 in) and the thickness varies between 5.2 millimetres (0.20 in) and 2.4 millimetres (0.094 in).[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-99) Because of the high value of their gold content and tendency to be on public display, Nobel medals are subject to medal theft.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-UniversityofCalifornia-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-NYTimes-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Reuters-102) During World War II, the medals of German scientists [Max von Laue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_von_Laue "Max von Laue") and [James Franck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Franck "James Franck") were sent to Copenhagen for safekeeping. When Germany invaded Denmark, Hungarian chemist (and Nobel laureate himself) [George de Hevesy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_de_Hevesy "George de Hevesy") dissolved them in [aqua regia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_regia "Aqua regia") (nitro-hydrochloric acid), to prevent confiscation by [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") and to prevent legal problems for the holders. After the war, the gold was recovered from solution, and the medals re-cast.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman397-103)

### Diplomas

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Nobel_Prize_diplom_Wilhelm_Conrad_R%C3%B6ntgen.jpg/250px-Nobel_Prize_diplom_Wilhelm_Conrad_R%C3%B6ntgen.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel_Prize_diplom_Wilhelm_Conrad_R%C3%B6ntgen.jpg)

The Nobel diploma awarded to [Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Conrad_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen") in 1901

Nobel laureates receive a diploma directly from the hands of the King of Sweden, or in the case of the peace prize, the chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. Each diploma is uniquely designed by the prize-awarding institutions for the laureates that receive them.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman2-97) The diploma contains a picture and text in Swedish which states the name of the laureate and normally a citation of why they received the prize. None of the Nobel Peace Prize laureates has ever had a citation on their diplomas.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams18-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-105)

### Award money

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Nobel_Prize_-_Prize_money_%281901-2023%29.svg/250px-Nobel_Prize_-_Prize_money_%281901-2023%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nobel_Prize_-_Prize_money_(1901-2023).svg)

Evolution of the prize amount between 1901 and 2023, adjusted for inflation

The laureates are given a sum of money when they receive their prizes, in the form of a document confirming the amount awarded.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman2-97) The amount of prize money depends upon how much money the Nobel Foundation can award each year. The purse has increased since the 1980s, when the prize money was 880,000 SEK per prize (c. 2.6 million SEK altogether, US$350,000 today). In 2009, the monetary award was 10 million SEK (US$1.4 million).[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Nobel_Prize_Amounts-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-CNN-107) In June 2012, it was lowered to 8 million SEK.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-108) If two laureates share the prize in a category, the award grant is divided equally between the recipients. If there are three, the awarding committee has the option of dividing the grant equally, or awarding one-half to one recipient and one-quarter to each of the others.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams8-10-109)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-111) It is common for recipients to donate prize money to benefit scientific, cultural, or humanitarian causes.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-113) As of 2026, the monetary award per prize category is 12 million Swedish kronor (SEK), equivalent to approximately US$1.221 million.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-PrizeMoney-114)

## Specially distinguished laureates

### Multiple laureates

[![Image 18: A black and white portrait of a woman in profile.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/93/Marie_Curie_1903.jpg/250px-Marie_Curie_1903.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marie_Curie_1903.jpg)

[Marie Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Sk%C5%82odowska-Curie "Marie Skłodowska-Curie"), one of five people who have received the Nobel Prize twice (Physics and Chemistry)

Five people have received two Nobel Prizes. [Marie Skłodowska-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Sk%C5%82odowska-Curie "Marie Skłodowska-Curie") received the Physics Prize in 1903 for her work on [radioactivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_decay "Radioactive decay") and the Chemistry Prize in 1911 for the isolation of pure [radium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radium "Radium"),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-117) making her the only person to be awarded a Nobel Prize in two different sciences. [Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling "Linus Pauling") was awarded the 1954 Chemistry Prize for his research into the [chemical bond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond "Chemical bond") and its application to the [structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_structure "Chemical structure") of complex substances. Pauling was also awarded the Peace Prize in 1962 for his activism against nuclear weapons, making him the only laureate of two unshared prizes. [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") received the Physics Prize twice: in 1956 for the invention of the [transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor "Transistor") and in 1972 for the theory of [superconductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superconductivity "Superconductivity").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman180-118)[Frederick Sanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Sanger "Frederick Sanger") received the prize twice in Chemistry: in 1958 for determining the structure of the [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") molecule and in 1980 for inventing a method of determining [base sequences in DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA_sequencing "DNA sequencing").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Shalev78-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman222-120)[Karl Barry Sharpless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Barry_Sharpless "Karl Barry Sharpless") was awarded the 2001 Chemistry Prize for his research into chirally catalysed oxidation reactions, and the 2022 Chemistry Prize for [click chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Click_chemistry "Click chemistry").

Two organisations have received the Peace Prize multiple times. The [International Committee of the Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Committee_of_the_Red_Cross "International Committee of the Red Cross") received it three times: in 1917 and 1944 for its work during the world wars; and in 1963 during the year of its centenary.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams84-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams149-122)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Abrams199-200-123) The [United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Refugees "United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees") has been awarded the Peace Prize twice for assisting refugees: in 1954 and 1981.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman313-124)

### Family laureates

The [Curie family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curie_family "Curie family") has received the most prizes, with four prizes awarded to five individual laureates. Her husband, [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie "Pierre Curie"), shared the 1903 Physics prize with her.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-125) Their daughter, [Irène Joliot-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ir%C3%A8ne_Joliot-Curie "Irène Joliot-Curie"), received the Chemistry Prize in 1935 together with her husband [Frédéric Joliot-Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Joliot-Curie "Frédéric Joliot-Curie"). In addition, [Henry Labouisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Richardson_Labouisse_Jr. "Henry Richardson Labouisse Jr."), the husband of Marie and Pierre Curie's second daughter [Ève Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%88ve_Curie "Ève Curie"), was the director of [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF") when he accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965 on that organisation's behalf.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize#cite_note-Feldman405-126)

## Abstract

### Aims

To analyze the main contributions to the discovery of the antidiabetic hormone in the period between 1889, the year in which Oskar Minkowski demonstrated that complete pancreatectomy in dogs caused diabetes, and the year 1923, the date in which the clinical use of insulin was consolidated. A main objective has been to review the controversies that followed the Nobel Prize and to outline the role of the priority rule in Science.

### Methods

We have considered the priority rule defined by Robert Merton in 1957, which takes into account the date of acceptance of the report of a discovery in an accredited scientific journal and/or the granting of a patent, complemented by the criteria set out by Ronald Vale and Anthony Hyman (2016) regarding the transfer of information to the scientific community and its validation by it. The awarding of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in October 1923 has represented a frame of reference. The claims and disputes regarding the prioritization of the contributions of the main researchers in the organotherapy of diabetes have been analyzed through the study of their scientific production and the debate generated in academic institutions.

### Main results and conclusions

(1) According to the criteria of Merton, Vale and Hyman, the priority of the discovery of the antidiabetic hormone corresponds to the investigations developed in Europe by E. Gley (1900), GL Zülzer (1908) and NC Paulescu (1920). (2) The active principle of the pancreatic extracts developed by Zülzer (acomatol), Paulescu (pancreina) and Banting and Best (insulin) was the same. (3) JB Collip succeeded in isolating the active ingredient from the pancreatic extract in January 1922, eliminating impurities to the point of enabling its use in the clinic. (4) In 1972, the Nobel Foundation modified the purpose of the 1923 Physiology or Medicine award to Banting and Macleod by introducing a new wording: "the credit for having produced the pancreatic hormone in a practical available form" (instead of “for the discovery of insulin”).

## Alfred Nobel's Testament (1895)

On November 27, 1895, a year before his death from a cerebral hemorrhage, Alfred Nobel (1833–1896) dictated his will at the Swedish-Norwegian club in Paris, by which he bequeathed to his relatives (he did not marry or have children) a legacy of 100,000 crowns. The rest of his fortune (about 33 million crowns) was allocated to the annual award of the Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature and Peace Prizes (Figs. 1, 2) [1, 2].Fig. 1Portrait of Alfred Nobel. Unknown date and author [1]. Public domainFig. 2Testament of Alfred Nobel [2]. Public domain

## The award of the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine

Jan Lindstein and Nils Ringertz have described in depth the procedure followed in the election of the Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine in the period between 1901 and 2000 [3].

The activity regarding the awarding of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is carried out by the Nobel Committee, elected by the Nobel Assembly from among its members, all of whom are professors at the Karolinska Institute. The Nobel Assembly is independent, both from the legal point of view and from the economic-administrative. Funding for the prizes comes exclusively from the Nobel Foundation. The Nobel Assembly has freedom to reward, indistinctly, areas in the broad field of biomedical research and clinical medicine. The prize is awarded for an extraordinary discovery and not for a scientific career of a lifetime. The concession must recognize a contribution or discovery of the highest level made during the previous year, a very difficult standard to meet, since the discovery must be published, known and evaluated by a group of internationally qualified researchers, a process that rarely lasts less than one year. To solve this dilemma, the pragmatic solution was to interpret that what matters is that _the benefit of the discovery has become evident to the members of the Nobel Assembly during the year preceding the date of the award._

In the month of September of the year prior to the awarding of the prize, invitations are sent to some 3,000 scientists from non-Scandinavian universities and academic institutions chosen by a rotating system, to make proposals for appointments. Proposals must be made according to a model sent by the Nobel Committee. Scientists previously recipients of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine and professors at medical schools in the Nordic countries can exercise their right to make proposals each year. The deadline for submitting proposals is January 31 of the year of the award. Between the months of March and May, the Nobel Committee invites international experts to submit their reports. All candidates are evaluated by members of the Nobel Assembly and external reviewers; the evaluations are sent before the end of August. In September, the Nobel Committee sends its recommendations on potential candidates to the Nobel Assembly. In the month of October, the election takes place by majority vote. This decision is final, with no possibility of appeal. The laureates are immediately informed and the decision is announced at a press conference. The Nobel Prize award ceremony takes place on December 10 in Stockholm, during which the laureates receive a gold medal, a diploma and a monetary award.

### Influence of August Krogh in awarding the Nobel Prize to Banting and Macleod

Schack August Stenberg Krogh (1874–1949) received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1920 "for his discovery of the regulatory mechanisms of capillary circulation".

His wife, Dr. Birte Marie Krogh, was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus in 1921, under the medical care of Dr. Hans Christian Hagedorn (1868–1971). In 1922, Krogh received an invitation to give several lectures in the USA. In November, in Boston, Dr. Elliot P. Joslin briefed him on research from the University of Toronto into the therapeutic benefits and purification process of insulin. On October 23, 1922, Krogh wrote to Macleod from Minneapolis, informing him of his interest in investigating the actions of the pancreatic extract and producing insulin in Denmark. Macleod immediately responded in favorable terms (Fig.3).Fig. 3August Krogh sent this letter to JJR Macleod on October 23, 1922, proposing a possible collaboration with HC Hagedorn to extend insulin production and therapeutic trials to the University of Copenhagen (Archives of the University of Toronto Library)

Krogh decided to extend his trip, going to Toronto as a guest of Prof. JJR Macleod. He returned to Copenhagen in December 1922. Marie successfully started her insulin treatment in December 1922, and Krogh obtained the license from the University of Toronto to produce insulin in Scandinavia (Suppl. Fig. 1).

The day after their arrival in Denmark, Krogh and Hagedorn began an intensive investigative process. The first experiments were carried out in Hagedorn's own house and in the laboratory of the Institute of Zoology, directed by Krogh. Very soon, on December 21, 1922, they successfully obtained a small amount of insulin from bovine pancreas. Immediately, August Krogh and Hans Christian Hagedorn founded the Nordisk Insulin Laboratory company, with the financial contribution of August Kongsted (1870–1939), pharmacist and owner of the company Løvens Kemiske Fabrik (Leo Pharmaceutical Products). Kongsted financed the research and production process. In compensation for such an important contribution, the condition requested by Kongsted was to name the first manufactured product "Insulin Leo", which became available in the spring of 1923. The first Danish patient treated with “Insulin Leo” received his initial dose on March 13, 1923.

Prof. August Krogh and Prof. Göran Liljestrand (Executive Secretary of the Nobel Committee since 1918) were friends. Their relationship intensified after Liljestrand did an academic stay in Copenhagen. On January 20, 1923, Krogh wrote a letter to Göran Liljestrand, in the following terms (Suppl. Fig. 2):As you understand from my discourse, it is my opinion that the discovery of insulin is of extraordinary both theoretical and practical importance and it will hardly surprise you that I intend to submit a nomination that the Nobel Prize be awarded to Dr. Banting and Professor Macleod.

The Nobel Committee for the award of Physiology or Medicine of the year 1923 consisted of 5 members, in addition to its president and executive secretary (Prof. Göran Liljestrand). The Archives of the Karolinska Institutet received within the stipulated period the joint proposal of August Krogh in favor of FG Banting and JJR Macleod, and the individual proposals of Francis G Benedict (Prof. of Physiology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Mass., USA) and Georg W Crile (Prof. of Surgery, University of Cleveland, Ohio, USA), on behalf of FG Banting; and Georg N. Stewart (Professor of Experimental Medicine, Case Western Reserve University, Cleveland) on behalf of JJR Macleod.

August Krogh reasoned his joint proposal of Macleod and Banting in the following terms:With the information which I personally have obtained in Toronto, and which also, although less clearly so, emerges from the published works, one may conclude that the credit for the idea behind the work which led to the discovery undoubtedly goes to Banting, who is a young and apparently very talented man. However, he would definitely not have been able to carry out the investigations, which from the start and during all stages have been supervised by Professor Macleod.

Macleod's special contributions to experimental work had only been partially published before the January 31, 1923, deadline. Macleod, working alone, had located insulin in the pancreas of teleost fish, demonstrating its hormonal function; he had also conducted investigations of the insulin actions on intermediary metabolism and respiratory quotient. Written reports on the proposals were prepared by two members of the Nobel Committee, John Sjöqvist, Professor of Chemistry and Pharmacy, and Hans Christian Jacobeus, Professor of Internal Medicine. Sjöqvist focused primarily on its physiological importance. He discussed the work of several predecessors, especially Georg Ludwig Zülzer. In his conclusion, he supported the joint request of A. Krogh, accepting the suggestion of dividing the prize between Banting and Macleod. Banting had the original idea and the first initiative; Macleod was the leader of the scientific work. Jacobeus’ decision was more difficult because “Macleod’s contribution was not apparent from the consulted bibliography” [2]. He then continued: “Banting came to Macleod with his idea… it is very likely that the discovery would not have been made if Macleod had not supervised him, at least not as rapidly as is now the case… I am most prone to give Banting and Macleod a joint Nobel Prize” [4].

After the Nobel Assembly had discussed the matter, the recommendation was sent back to the Committee for reconsideration on October 11, 1923. The objection responded to the need to verify the foundations of Krogh’s joint proposal, based on his visit to Toronto [5].

The Committee met again, reaffirmed his recommendation and made an extensive written statement to finally conclude that “… it is not possible to make a more thorough investigation of this discovery and the relative contributions by Banting and Macleod, nor is it necessary” [6].

The Committee considered valid the argument that although the discovery corresponded, initially, to Banting's idea, Macleod's guidance was decisive for its successful fulfillment. Finally, the nineteen professors of the Karolinska Institutet cast their secret ballot, ruling that “The Nobel Award of Physiology and Medicine was jointly granted on October 25, 1923, to Frederick Grant Banting and John James Rickard Macleod, for the discovery of insulin, one year before” [7].

It is logical to assume that Krogh's influence on Macleod's candidacy for the Nobel Prize was manifest, particularly as Krogh was previously laureated in 1920 and was informed by Macleod in Toronto on the scientific activities carried out in situ, benefiting from the license of the University of Toronto to produce insulin in Denmark [8].

Frederick G. Banting learned of the Nobel Prize award on the morning of October 26, 1923, from the front page of The Globe newspaper (Fig.4).Fig. 4Front page of _The Globe_ newspaper, October 23, 1923, reporting the award of the Nobel Prize in Medicine to Doctors Banting and Macleod

Banting was furious about having to share the award with JJR Macleod, and his first intention was to reject the prize. JG Fitzgerald, director of Connaught Laboratories, tried to persuade him. Banting’s answer was: “I will not accept the prize: I am going to cable Stockholm that not only would I not accept but that they and the old foggy Krogh could go to hell…I defied you to name one idea that had originated in Macleod’s brain – or to name one experiment he had done with his own hands”.

Fitzgerald was soon able to calm him and suggested he should meet Albert E. Gooderham, chairman of the Insulin Committee of the University of Toronto Board of Governors. Gooderham managed to convince Banting, arguing that other considerations deserved to be taken into account: “I must think of my country. What would the people of Canada think if the first Canadian to receive this honor were to turn it down? Banting did not say he will decide it immediately and better wait 24 h”. On October 26, Banting grabbed a notepad and wrote a telegram to Best (he was in Boston): “Nobel trustees have conferred prize on Macleod and me. You are with me in my share always” [9].

Banting decided to split 50% of the corresponding financial contribution with Charles H. Best. Macleod first heard the Nobel news on a steamship returning from Scotland to Canada. He decided also to split 50% of the corresponding amount with James B. Collip.

The monetary value of the prize in 1923 was 114,935 Swedish Crowns (SEK) (24,000 USD). This amount would be equivalent in 2021 to approximately 3,241,843 SEK (419,888 USD). In the years 2021–2022, the monetary value of the prize has reached 10 million SEK (1,103,148; USD; 964, 000 €) [10].

The University of Toronto celebrated the Nobel award with a special ceremony on November 26, 1923, in which both laureates, FG Banting and JJR Macleod, received the honorary degree of Doctor of Science. A banquet in the Great Hall of Start House that evening capped off the celebration with more than 400 guests representing the North American government, scientific, and medical professionals (Suppl. Fig. 3).

On December 10, 1923, Prof. J. Sjöquist, member of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, delivered the Presentation Lecture for the Nobel Prize to Dr. Frederick Grant Banting and Professor John James Rickard Macleod “by the discovery of insulin”. In the absence of the laureates, the British Minister received the prizes from the hands of His Majesty the King, for future transfer to them [11].

Banting took all possible actions to make unpleasant Macleod’s life. The Scottish Professor felt he had to start legal actions against Banting, but he finally decided to leave the University and the city of Toronto in 1928. When the University held a farewell dinner for Macleod, Banting not only refused to attend, he requested that there be an empty place set for him at the table [5].

## Discovery of the pancreatic origin of diabetes: Oskar Minkowski

In April 1889, Oskar Minkowski, of the Department of Medicine at the University of Strasbourg (directed by Professor Naunyn), met Joseph von Mering in the library of the Hoppe-Seyler's Institute, University of Strasbourg. In 1886, von Mering had generated experimental diabetes with the administration of phloridzin and was then investigating the enzymatic function of the pancreas in the digestion of fatty foods.

Minkowski suggested that to achieve this goal it would be highly desirable to investigate the effects of total pancreatectomy and was able to overcome initial resistance from von Mering, who felt that such surgery was impossible to perform successfully. That same day they agreed that Minkowski would perform, with Mering's help, a complete pancreatectomy in the experimental laboratory of the Department of Medicine on one of the dogs at Hoppe Seyler's laboratory. After the first pancreatectomy, Mering did not participate in further research on this matter, directing his excellent academic career elsewhere. Minkowski reproduced the effects of complete pancreatectomy in three other dogs. The first two died, but the third survived and in less than 48 h presented glycosuria, polydipsia and polyuria. In the weeks following surgery, gradual weight loss was observed in spite of excessive energy intake, also showing persistent glycosuria, ketonuria and hyperglycemia.

Minkowski presented the first paper at the International Congress of Physiology in Basel. The first publication was a short communication in 1889 [12]. More extensive reports appeared in 1890, 1892 and 1893 [13–15].

Minkowski and Naunyn had previously shown that beta-hydroxybutyric acid is an agent responsible for diabetic acidosis and that the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood markedly decreases in this acute metabolic emergency [16].

Rolf Luft (1914–2007), Professor of Endocrinology, Karolinska Hospital, Stockholm, in asking who discovered insulin declared that “Minkowski was the first to show that diabetes is the consequence of the absence of the pancreatic substance carried by the bloodstream, which motivated all the subsequent activities aimed at extracting the antidiabetic hormone. It has been the most important original discovery in the history of diabetes” [17].

## Protests over the awarding of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1923

The decision of the 19 signatories from the Karolinska Institutet was protested in subsequent weeks and months by at least four researchers, who claimed their priority in isolating the antidiabetic hormone: Georg Ludwig Zülzer (Berlin), Ernest Lyman Scott (Chicago), John Raymond Murlin (New York) and Nicolae Constantin Paulescu (Bucharest).
